title: Builds with Gradle
intro: You use Gradle every day through IntelliJ, but in DevOps work you run builds where there is no IDE: on CI runners and inside Docker builds. This part teaches Gradle's model from the ground up with a new lab, hello-jvm, a small Kotlin web service that mirrors hello-devops. It comes after Docker and GitHub Actions because Day 24 uses both to build, cache and ship that service.

lessons.title: What a build tool does, and how Gradle thinks
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain Gradle's model of projects, tasks and phases, create a project with the Gradle Wrapper, and predict which tasks a build will run or skip.

guess.q: You run `./gradlew test`, change nothing, and run it again. What does Gradle do with the tests the second time?
options: Compiles everything again and reruns every test
Reruns only the tests that failed last time
Skips the test task and marks it UP-TO-DATE
Asks you whether the tests should run again
guess.why: Gradle fingerprints every task's inputs and outputs. Nothing changed, so the last results still hold and the task is skipped; `--rerun` forces it to run.

sections.h: What a build tool does
sections.body:
Turning Kotlin source into something you can ship takes more steps than it looks. For one small web service you have to:

- download the libraries it uses, and the libraries those libraries use
- compile the Kotlin code against them
- compile and run the tests
- package the classes into a jar, with start scripts
- do all of it the same way on your laptop and on the CI server

A shell script that calls `kotlinc` and `java` works for one file. Then the classpath grows to 40 jars, a teammate has another JDK, and every run recompiles everything because the script cannot tell what changed.

A **build tool** does these jobs from a description of the project that lives in git. Gradle is the one most Kotlin and Android projects use, and you already use it every day through IntelliJ. This lesson opens the box. In DevOps work you run builds where there is no IDE: on CI runners, in Docker build stages and in release jobs. There you need to know what Gradle is doing and why.

sections.h: Tasks and the task graph
sections.body:
Gradle's unit of work is a task. A task has a name such as `compileKotlin`, `test` or `jar`. It also declares its inputs (source files, the classpath, compiler flags) and its outputs (class files, a jar, a test report).

Tasks depend on other tasks. `jar` needs compiled classes, so it depends on `classes`, which depends on `compileKotlin`. When you ask for `build`, Gradle collects every task it needs and puts them in a task graph. The graph is a DAG (directed acyclic graph): the arrows point one way and never loop back. Gradle runs each task once, in an order that respects the arrows. `build` itself does no work. It groups `assemble`, which makes the outputs, and `check`, which runs the tests.

Declaring inputs and outputs pays off on the second run. Before a task runs, Gradle fingerprints its inputs and outputs and compares them with the last run. If nothing changed, it prints `UP-TO-DATE` and skips the task. You will see these labels on task lines:

- `UP-TO-DATE`: nothing changed since the last run, so the task was skipped.
- `NO-SOURCE`: there was nothing to work on, like `compileJava` in a Kotlin-only project.
- `SKIPPED`: skipped on purpose, for example under `--dry-run`.
- `FROM-CACHE`: the outputs were copied from the build cache (Day 24).

No label means the task did real work.

sections.h: Projects, plugins and the build files
sections.body:
A Gradle build is a set of projects. A project is usually one folder with its own build script. Today your hello-jvm build has a root project and one subproject, `app`. Tomorrow you add a second one.

Three files describe the build:

- `settings.gradle.kts` is read first, once per build. It names the build, lists the projects with `include(...)`, and says where libraries come from.
- `build.gradle.kts` is the build script of one project. It applies plugins and lists the libraries the project needs.
- `gradle.properties` holds flags for Gradle itself, such as turning on the configuration cache.

The `.kts` ending means Kotlin script. This is the Kotlin DSL: the build files are real Kotlin, so IntelliJ autocompletes them and the compiler catches typos. Older projects use `build.gradle` files written in Groovy. They do the same job with looser syntax. Since Gradle 8, `gradle init` writes Kotlin build files by default.

On its own a build script does very little. Plugins bring the tasks. In `app/build.gradle.kts`, `kotlin("jvm")` adds `compileKotlin`, `test` and `jar`, and the `application` plugin adds `run`, `installDist` and start scripts. That is why `./gradlew tasks` lists more than 30 tasks for a build script with a dozen real lines.

sections.h: Three phases: initialization, configuration, execution
sections.body:
This is the idea that trips up most people, so take it slowly. Every Gradle run goes through three phases, in this order:

1. Initialization. Gradle reads `settings.gradle.kts` and decides which projects take part.
2. Configuration. Gradle runs the build scripts of those projects. The scripts register tasks and set their properties, and Gradle builds the task graph for what you asked.
3. Execution. Gradle runs the actions of the tasks in the graph, in dependency order.

Here is the trap. A build script does not do the work; it describes the work. Code at the top level of `build.gradle.kts` runs during configuration. So does code inside `tasks.register("x") { ... }`. Only the code inside `doLast { ... }` runs when the task executes. A `println` at the top of a build script prints before any task starts.

`tasks.register` is lazy: Gradle only sets up a task when the graph needs it. Still, keep slow work out of configuration. No network calls, no big file reads, no running programs at the top level. Configuration happens on every run that is not cached, even `./gradlew help`.

Gradle 9 adds the configuration cache. It saves the result of phases 1 and 2, and the next run with the same scripts and tasks goes straight to execution. In return, a running task may not reach back into `project`, the live build model. The worked example shows the error and the fix.

sections.h: The Gradle Wrapper: one Gradle version per project
sections.body:
You will almost never type `gradle`. You type `./gradlew`. That script is the **Gradle Wrapper**, and it is why a fresh clone builds the same way on every machine. The wrapper is four files, and you commit all of them:

- `gradlew`, a shell script for macOS and Linux
- `gradlew.bat`, the same for Windows
- `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar`, a small program that downloads Gradle
- `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, which names the exact Gradle version

On the first run, `./gradlew` downloads that version into `~/.gradle/wrapper/dists`. After that, you, your teammates and every CI runner use the same Gradle. Think of it as a lockfile for the build tool. A global `gradle` from Homebrew is whatever version you installed last, and Gradle 9 removed several old APIs. A build can pass on 8.14 and fail on 9.8, or the other way round.

You need a global Gradle only once, to create the wrapper in a new project with `gradle wrapper` (or `gradle init`). Add `--gradle-distribution-sha256-sum` and the wrapper checks every download against that checksum and refuses anything else. To upgrade later, run `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version <new version>`.

Two JDKs are in play. Gradle 9 itself needs Java 17 or newer to run. The JDK that compiles your code is picked separately, by `kotlin { jvmToolchain(21) }` in the build script. Day 24 covers toolchains.

sections.h: Running tasks and reading the output
sections.body:
Run any task by name: `./gradlew build`, `./gradlew test`, `./gradlew clean`. In a build with several projects, a bare name runs that task in every project that has it. A path picks one project: `./gradlew :app:run` runs `run` in `app` only. The first colon means the root project, like `/` in a file path.

These options come up every week:

- `./gradlew tasks` lists the tasks you can run, by group. `--all` shows every task.
- `./gradlew help --task :app:run` explains one task and its options.
- `--dry-run` lists what would run, without running it.
- `--task-graph` prints the graph as a tree.
- `-q` hides everything except errors and your program's own output.
- `--console=plain` prints one plain line per task, which reads better in CI logs.
- `--args="..."` passes arguments to your program in `./gradlew :app:run`.

Read the output from the bottom. `BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 7s` or `BUILD FAILED` comes last. Above it, a line like `7 actionable tasks: 7 executed` says how many tasks did work and how many were up to date. When a test fails, Gradle prints the path of an HTML report, such as `app/build/reports/tests/test/index.html`. Open it in your browser: it shows each test, its output and the stack trace.

sections.h: Gradle and Maven, briefly
sections.body:
You will meet Maven at work, often in older Java services. Both tools download from the same repositories, such as Maven Central, and both produce the same kind of jar. The model is what differs:

- Maven describes a project in XML (`pom.xml`) and runs a fixed list of phases, such as `compile`, `test`, `package` and `install`. `mvn package` runs every phase up to `package`.
- Gradle builds a graph of tasks from Kotlin or Groovy scripts, and skips each task whose inputs did not change.
- Maven has a wrapper too, `mvnw`, for the same reason Gradle has `gradlew`.
- Rough mapping: `mvn package` is close to `./gradlew assemble`, `mvn verify` is close to `./gradlew build`, and `mvn dependency:tree` is `./gradlew dependencies`.

For one plain service, neither tool is clearly better. Gradle pulls ahead in big builds, because it reuses so much earlier work (Day 24 shows how). Android builds require Gradle. Spring Initializr offers both, so the choice was usually made before you joined the team. As a DevOps engineer you need to read both and run both in CI.

lessons.analogy: Gradle works like a careful cook with a recipe book. First the cook reads the recipes for tonight's menu and writes down which dish needs which (configuration). Then the cook works through that list in order (execution). If a sauce from an hour ago was made from exactly the same ingredients, the cook uses it again instead of making it twice (UP-TO-DATE). Where it breaks: a cook judges by eye, while Gradle compares exact fingerprints of every input file, so one changed byte means the task runs again.

lessons.mistake: Running `gradle build` with a global Gradle instead of `./gradlew build`. The global one is whatever version you installed last, so the build can pass for you and fail in CI, or the other way round. Always run `./gradlew`, and keep IntelliJ on the wrapper (its default). Use a global Gradle only to create the wrapper once.
lessons.real_world: At a payments company (call it Paylane), the ledger service has many Gradle projects, and CI runs `./gradlew build` on every pull request. The wrapper pins Gradle, so laptops and runners agree, and a Gradle upgrade is an ordinary pull request that changes `gradle-wrapper.properties`. When CI gets slow, the first thing the team reads is which tasks did work and which were UP-TO-DATE or FROM-CACHE.

explain_back.prompt: Explain Gradle's three phases in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention when a `println` at the top of build.gradle.kts runs, and what the configuration cache lets Gradle skip.
explain_back.answer: First Gradle reads the settings file to find out which projects are in the build. Then it runs the build scripts of those projects, which register and set up tasks, and it builds a graph of the tasks I asked for. Only after that does it run the tasks' actions, in dependency order. A `println` at the top of a build script runs in the configuration phase, before any task starts. The configuration cache saves the task graph, so a repeat run with the same scripts skips the first two phases and goes straight to execution.

During configuration, before any task runs

check.q: `./gradlew :app:jar` prints `> Task :app:compileKotlin UP-TO-DATE` and then `> Task :app:jar` with no label. What happened?
options: Compiling was skipped; the jar was rebuilt
Compiling failed without an error message
Neither task did any work this time
Both outputs came from another machine
check.why: UP-TO-DATE means skipped because nothing changed, and a task line with no label did real work (here, perhaps because the old jar was deleted).

interview.q: What is the Gradle Wrapper, and why commit it?
interview.a: The wrapper is the `gradlew` script, a small jar and a properties file that names one Gradle version. Running `./gradlew` downloads exactly that version and uses it, so every developer and CI runner builds with the same Gradle. You commit all four files so a fresh clone needs only a JDK. I also set `distributionSha256Sum`, so a tampered download is refused, and upgrades become a reviewed one-line change.

interview.q: Walk me through Gradle's build lifecycle.
interview.a: Initialization reads the settings file and decides which projects take part. Configuration runs their build scripts, which register tasks, and Gradle builds the task graph for the requested tasks. Execution runs the task actions in dependency order and skips tasks whose inputs and outputs are unchanged. The common mistake is heavy work at configuration time, which slows every run, even `help`. The configuration cache skips the first two phases when nothing relevant changed.

interview.q: How does Gradle decide that a task is UP-TO-DATE?
interview.a: Each task declares inputs, such as source files, the classpath and flags, and outputs, such as class files. After a run, Gradle stores fingerprints of both. Next time it compares fresh fingerprints with the stored ones, and if nothing differs and the outputs are still there, it skips the task. A task that declares no outputs can never be up to date, so it always runs.

deeper.body:
Gradle does not guess when it skips a task. Ask it why a task ran with `--info`. After adding a comment to `Main.kt`, `./gradlew :app:compileKotlin --info` printed:

- `Task ':app:compileKotlin' is not up-to-date because:`
- `Input property 'sources' file .../app/src/main/kotlin/hello/app/Main.kt has changed.`

So what goes into the comparison? Four things:

1. Input files, by content hash. Timestamps do not matter: `touch Main.kt` leaves all 7 tasks up to date, while one changed byte does not.
2. Input properties, such as the JVM target or compiler flags.
3. The task's own code. Upgrade the Kotlin plugin and every Kotlin compile task runs again.
4. Output files. Delete `app/build/libs/app.jar` and only `jar` runs again. The tasks after it stay up to date, because Gradle 9 builds the same jar byte for byte.

This explains a few things you will see. A task with no declared outputs, like `hello` in the worked example, always runs. A test-only change runs `compileTestKotlin` and `test`, but `compileKotlin` and `jar` stay up to date, because their inputs are the main source files only. And a task's outputs are the next task's inputs. If `compileKotlin` runs but produces byte-for-byte the same class files, the tasks after it can still be skipped. Day 24 uses that to explain compile avoidance across projects.

Two flags force work. The `--rerun` flag reruns the one task you name, for example `./gradlew test --rerun` when you suspect a flaky test. The `--rerun-tasks` flag reruns every task in the graph, which is slow and almost never what you want. If you reach for it often, a task is probably missing an input, and the real fix is in the build logic.

One more habit worth building now: when a build surprises you, read the task lines before you read the error. They tell you what Gradle thought had changed. If you want to see the whole graph first, `--task-graph` prints it without running anything.

lessons.title: Dependencies and multi-project builds
lessons.goal: By the end you can declare dependencies in the right configuration, explain which version Gradle picked and why, and split a build into projects that share a version catalog and a convention plugin.

guess.q: Your app asks for commons-lang3 3.17.0. A library your app uses needs commons-lang3 3.18.0. Which version is on the app's runtime classpath?
options: 3.17.0, because your own declaration wins
3.18.0, because Gradle picks the highest
Both, each library gets its own copy
Neither: the build stops with a conflict
guess.why: When two versions of one library meet, Gradle picks the highest by default. Maven picks the declaration nearest your project instead, so the same dependencies can resolve differently there.

sections.h: Repositories and coordinates
sections.body:
A dependency is a library your code needs, such as JUnit or a JSON parser. To fetch one, Gradle needs two facts: where to look and what to ask for.

Where to look is a repository, a server that stores published jars with their metadata. You will meet three kinds:

- Maven Central (`mavenCentral()`), where most open-source JVM libraries live
- the Gradle Plugin Portal (`gradlePluginPortal()`), where most Gradle plugins live
- your company's own repository, often a mirror of both (Nexus or Artifactory)

What to ask for is the coordinates: group, name and version in one string. `org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3` has the group `org.junit`, the name `junit-bom` and the version `6.1.3`. Maven uses the same coordinates. Gradle downloads each file once into `~/.gradle/caches/modules-2` and reuses it in every project on your laptop.

Declare repositories once, in `settings.gradle.kts`. In hello-jvm, `repositoriesMode = RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS` fails the build if a project adds its own. That sounds strict, but at work it is what you want. There is one place to point at the company mirror, and no project can quietly pull from a random server.

sections.h: Configurations: which classpath a dependency joins
sections.body:
You never add a dependency to a project in general. You add it to a configuration, and the configuration decides which classpaths it joins. A classpath is the list of jars that the compiler or the JVM can see. Each project has one for compiling the main code, one for running it, and the same two for tests. The configurations you will use:

- `implementation`: needed to compile and run this project. Projects that use yours cannot see it when they compile.
- `api`: like `implementation`, but also on the compile classpath of every project that uses yours. It needs the `java-library` plugin.
- `compileOnly`: needed to compile, but provided by someone else at runtime.
- `runtimeOnly`: needed only when the program runs, such as a database driver.
- `testImplementation` and `testRuntimeOnly`: the same ideas, for the tests.

Make `implementation` your default. It keeps a library's insides private: a consumer cannot import a class from a library you only use internally. It also saves build time. When you upgrade an `implementation` dependency, the projects that use yours do not recompile.

Use `api` only when a type from that library appears in your public functions. If your function returns a `Money` from a money library, every caller needs that library to compile, so it is part of your API.

sections.h: Transitive dependencies and highest-wins
sections.body:
Libraries have dependencies of their own. Ask for `commons-text` and you also get `commons-lang3`, because `commons-text` needs it. These are transitive dependencies, and in a real service they often outnumber the ones you declared.

Sooner or later, two paths ask for different versions of the same library. Gradle settles this conflict with one rule: the highest version wins. Your own declaration gets no extra weight. This surprises people who know Maven, where the declaration nearest your project wins.

Two reports show what really happened:

- `./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath` prints the whole tree. An arrow such as `3.17.0 -> 3.18.0` means one version was asked for and another was chosen. `(*)` marks a subtree already printed above.
- `./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --dependency commons-lang3 --configuration runtimeClasspath` explains one library: the version picked, the reason (such as `By conflict resolution`) and every path that asked for it.

Gradle resolves each classpath separately. So the compile classpath can hold 3.17.0 while the runtime classpath holds 3.18.0. The worked example shows exactly that, and the deeper section shows how to make the two agree.

sections.h: Version catalogs: one file for names and versions
sections.body:
In a build with ten projects, the same version string ends up in ten build files, and one upgrade means ten edits. A version catalog fixes that. It is a TOML file at `gradle/libs.versions.toml`, and Gradle reads it automatically. It has up to four sections:

- `[versions]`: named version numbers, such as `kotlin = "2.4.21"`
- `[libraries]`: short names for coordinates, such as `junit-bom`
- `[bundles]`: groups of libraries you often add together
- `[plugins]`: names for plugins and their versions

Build scripts then say `libs.junit.bom` instead of `"org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3"`, and `alias(libs.plugins.jib)` for a plugin. Dashes in names become dots. IntelliJ completes these names, and a typo fails the build at once instead of fetching the wrong thing.

Know what a catalog does not do. It only gives names to coordinates. It does not force any version onto the dependency graph, so highest-wins still decides the transitive ones. That job belongs to platforms, next.

sections.h: Platforms and BOMs: versions that move together
sections.body:
Some libraries come as a family of modules that must share one version. JUnit is one: `junit-jupiter-api`, `junit-jupiter-engine` and `junit-platform-launcher` have to match, or tests fail in confusing ways.

A BOM (bill of materials) is a published list of recommended versions for such a family. Gradle calls it a platform, and you add it like a dependency, wrapped in `platform(...)`. hello-jvm does this in its convention plugin: `testImplementation(platform(...junit-bom...))`.

Here is why. `kotlin("test")` pulls in `kotlin-test-junit5`, which asks for JUnit 5.10.1. The JUnit 6.1.3 BOM moves every JUnit module to 6.1.3. The dependency report shows it as `junit-jupiter-engine:5.10.1 -> 6.1.3`, with lines marked `(c)` for the BOM's constraints.

You will see BOMs all over the JVM world. Spring Boot and Jackson both publish one. A normal `platform()` takes part in highest-wins like everything else. `enforcedPlatform()` forces its versions, even downward. Use it rarely, because it can silently downgrade something a library needs.

sections.h: Multi-project builds
sections.body:
So far hello-jvm has one project. Today you split it in two:

- `greeting` is a library. It builds the JSON reply, escapes text properly, and knows nothing about HTTP.
- `app` is the web service. It depends on `greeting` and adds the server.

Why bother for a tiny service? The Day 22 version builds JSON by gluing strings. Start it with a `GREETING` that contains a double quote and `curl` returns `{"message":"Say "hi"",...}`, which no JSON parser accepts. Escaping is exactly the kind of logic that deserves its own module and its own tests. In a big codebase the same split gives clear boundaries and faster builds, because a change in `app` never recompiles `greeting`.

The wiring is two lines. `include("app", "greeting")` in the settings file declares both projects. `implementation(project(":greeting"))` in `app/build.gradle.kts` makes `app` use `greeting` like any library, except that Gradle builds it first.

Task paths matter now:

- `./gradlew build` at the root builds both projects.
- `./gradlew :greeting:test` tests only the library.
- `./gradlew :app:build` builds `app` and only the parts of `greeting` it needs, such as its jar.
- `./gradlew projects` prints the tree.

sections.h: Share setup with a convention plugin
sections.body:
Split a build and the build scripts start repeating themselves. Both projects need the Kotlin plugin, `jvmToolchain(21)`, kotlin.test, the JUnit BOM and `useJUnitPlatform()`. Copy that into ten projects and the copies drift apart. Older builds put shared setup in `allprojects {}` or `subprojects {}` blocks in the root script. Gradle now advises against that, because it ties every project to the root.

The current answer is a convention plugin: your own small plugin that holds the shared setup. In hello-jvm it lives in `build-logic`, a separate little Gradle build inside the repository:

1. `settings.gradle.kts` says `pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic") }`, so Gradle builds `build-logic` first and offers its plugins.
2. `build-logic/build.gradle.kts` applies `kotlin-dsl`, which turns each `*.gradle.kts` file in `src/main/kotlin` into a plugin.
3. The file `hello.kotlin-jvm.gradle.kts` becomes the plugin `hello.kotlin-jvm`.
4. Each project applies it with `id("hello.kotlin-jvm")`, and keeps only what is special about it.

Older projects often use a `buildSrc` folder for this. It works, but Gradle's best-practice guide prefers an included build like `build-logic`, partly because any change in `buildSrc` makes the whole build out of date.

Publishing a library takes one more plugin, `maven-publish`. Give `greeting` a `group` and `version`, and `./gradlew :greeting:publishToMavenLocal` installs it in `~/.m2`; other publish tasks push to a company repository. In the generated `pom.xml`, `api` dependencies get `compile` scope and `implementation` ones get `runtime` scope, so Maven users see the same split.

interview.q: What is the difference between api and implementation in Gradle?
interview.a: Both make a dependency available to the project that declares it. An `api` dependency is also exposed on the compile classpath of consumers, while `implementation` keeps it internal and only ships it at runtime. The `implementation` configuration is the default because it prevents accidental use of a library's internals and means fewer projects recompile when it changes. I use `api` only for libraries whose types appear in public signatures. It needs the `java-library` plugin.

interview.q: Two libraries need different versions of the same dependency. What does Gradle do, and how do you investigate?
interview.a: By default Gradle picks the highest requested version for the whole graph, unlike Maven's nearest-wins. I run `dependencies` on the relevant classpath to see arrows like `1.2 -> 1.4`, then `dependencyInsight` on that one module to get the selection reason and every path that asked for it. If the result is wrong, I declare the version I need, use a platform for families of libraries, or as a last resort a strict version.

interview.q: How would you share build configuration across many Gradle projects?
interview.a: I would write convention plugins as precompiled script plugins in an included build called `build-logic`, and apply them by id in each project. Versions go in the version catalog, which `build-logic` can read too. I avoid `allprojects` and `subprojects` blocks, because they couple every project to the root. Each project's own build script then only holds what is special about it.

deeper.body:
The worked example left a loose end. `app` compiled against commons-lang3 3.17.0 but ran with 3.18.0. Usually that is harmless, because libraries try to stay compatible within a major version. But if 3.18.0 changed a method you call, the code compiles fine and then fails at runtime with `NoSuchMethodError`. That is the worst kind of failure, because no build catches it.

You can make Gradle use the runtime versions when it compiles too. Add this to `app/build.gradle.kts`:

`java { consistentResolution { useRuntimeClasspathVersions() } }`

With that block, the compile classpath report for the same experiment showed `org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:3.17.0 -> 3.18.0`. `dependencyInsight` on the compile classpath gave a new reason: `By constraint: version resolved in configuration ':app:runtimeClasspath' by consistent resolution`. Now the compiler sees the jar that will really run.

Gradle has more tools for taking control of versions. Reach for them in this order:

1. Declare the version you need directly. Highest-wins then lifts every path in that project to it. This is the usual fix for a security alert.
2. Add a dependency constraint, such as `constraints { implementation("group:name:1.4.2") }`. It sets a version for a library you do not use directly, without adding it as a dependency. `gradle init` writes one of these in its generated builds.
3. Use a platform for a whole family, as hello-jvm does for JUnit.
4. As a last resort, use a strict version or `enforcedPlatform`, which can force a version downward. Check the graph afterwards, because you may have broken a library that needed the newer one.

There is also a switch for teams that want to decide every conflict by hand. With `configurations.runtimeClasspath { resolutionStrategy.failOnVersionConflict() }` in `app`, the dependency report marked both commons-lang3 entries `FAILED`. Put the same rule on every configuration with `configurations.all` and it fails first on the Kotlin compiler's own classpath, so keep it to the classpaths you care about.

Day 24 adds two more tools on top of all this. Dependency locking records the exact result of resolution in a file. Dependency verification checks the bytes of every downloaded jar.

sections.h: Four ways Gradle skips work
sections.body:
A slow build costs you on every run, on your laptop and on every CI job. Gradle's answer is to avoid repeating work, and it has four separate tricks. Keep them apart in your head:

- Up-to-date checks skip a task whose inputs and outputs did not change since the last run in the same folder (Day 22).
- The build cache copies a task's outputs from an earlier run anywhere, even in another folder or on another machine, when the inputs match.
- The configuration cache skips running the build scripts when they did not change.
- The daemon keeps a warm JVM between builds, so Gradle itself starts fast.

The Kotlin plugin adds compile avoidance on top. We changed `greeting` in three ways and watched `app`:

1. Add a comment: only `:greeting:compileKotlin` ran. It produced the same class files, so the jar and everything in `app` stayed UP-TO-DATE.
2. Change a function body: the `greeting` jar and both test tasks ran, but `:app:compileKotlin` stayed UP-TO-DATE. The ABI (the public signatures other code compiles against) had not changed.
3. Add a public function: now `:app:compileKotlin` ran too.

So a change behind a stable public API does not ripple through the build. That is one more reason to split code into projects and to prefer `implementation`.

sections.h: The build cache and the configuration cache
sections.body:
Turn the build cache on with `org.gradle.caching=true` in `gradle.properties`. Before a cacheable task runs, Gradle hashes all its inputs into a cache key. If the cache already holds outputs for that key, Gradle copies them in and prints `FROM-CACHE`. The folder path is not part of the key, so a fresh clone in another folder gets hits too. A fresh clone of hello-jvm on the same laptop built with `20 actionable tasks: 8 executed, 12 from cache`.

The local cache lives in `~/.gradle/caches/build-cache-1`. Many teams also run a remote cache, an HTTP server that every build can read. The usual setup is that CI writes to it and laptops only read. Pull main in the morning, and most of it is already compiled. Develocity, Gradle's commercial server, is one common choice.

The configuration cache is a different thing. It stores the task graph from Day 22's first two phases, keyed by your build files and the tasks you asked for. Gradle 9 calls it the preferred mode and plans to turn it on by default in Gradle 10. Two things to know:

- Some plugins are not compatible yet. They fail with `Invocation of 'Task.project' ... is unsupported with the configuration cache`, and `--no-configuration-cache` turns the cache off for one run.
- Entries can hold values from your build, including secrets, so treat the project's `.gradle` folder as private.
- A miss is only slower, never wrong: Gradle runs the scripts again and stores a new entry.

sections.h: The daemon, parallel builds and toolchains
sections.body:
The daemon is the background JVM behind `./gradlew`. The first build of the day starts one, which is why it is the slowest. Later builds reuse it, with classes already loaded and code already JIT-compiled. It stops after three idle hours. `./gradlew --status` lists daemons and `./gradlew --stop` stops them, the classic fix when builds act strangely after a JDK change. In CI, setup-gradle stops them at the end of a job that saves the cache.

`org.gradle.parallel=true` lets Gradle run tasks from different projects at the same time. hello-jvm is too small to notice. A build with dozens of projects can finish much sooner, because many projects only depend on a few others.

A toolchain separates the JDK that compiles your code from the JDK that runs Gradle. `kotlin { jvmToolchain(21) }` in the convention plugin asks for Java 21:

1. Gradle first looks for an installed JDK 21 (`./gradlew -q javaToolchains` lists what it found).
2. If there is none, the foojay plugin in `settings.gradle.kts` downloads one.
3. Compiling and testing then use that JDK, whatever `java -version` says in your terminal.

So your laptop can run Gradle on a newer Java and still compile for 21, and CI compiles with exactly the same version. This also explains the "works in IntelliJ, fails in the terminal" puzzle: there are two JDKs, and only one of them compiles your code.

sections.h: Trust: checksums, locking and Build Scans
sections.body:
Speed is half the job. The other half is knowing exactly what went into a build. Gradle has three tools for that, and each answers a different question:

- Is this the right Gradle? The wrapper's `distributionSha256Sum` refuses a download that does not match. We broke one character on purpose and got `Verification of Gradle distribution failed!`.
- Are these the same versions as last week? Dependency locking writes the exact resolved version of every library to `gradle.lockfile`. Turn it on with `dependencyLocking { lockAllConfigurations() }`, run `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`, and commit the file. A new version then fails the build, for example `Resolved 'org.opentest4j:opentest4j:1.3.0' which is not part of the dependency lock state`, until you update the lock on purpose.
- Are these the same bytes? Dependency verification keeps a SHA-256 checksum of every downloaded file in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Create it with `./gradlew --write-verification-metadata sha256 help`. A swapped jar then fails the build.

When a build is slow or flaky, a Build Scan shows why. Run `./gradlew build --scan`, and Gradle uploads a report of the run and prints a link. The report has task timings, test results and the dependency graph. The free service is scans.gradle.com. It asks you to accept its terms first, and your build data goes to Gradle's servers, so keep it for open code. Companies run their own Develocity server for private code, and since Gradle 9.5 `--develocity-url` points a build at one without editing it.

sections.h: Gradle in GitHub Actions
sections.body:
In CI you run the same command as on your laptop, `./gradlew build`. The workflow only prepares the runner, and `.github/workflows/jvm-ci.yml` does that in two steps:

1. `actions/setup-java` installs JDK 21, so the toolchain finds it and nothing extra is downloaded.
2. `gradle/actions/setup-gradle` does the Gradle work. It checks `gradle-wrapper.jar` against the checksums of real Gradle releases, so a tampered wrapper fails. It caches downloaded libraries, the wrapper's Gradle and the local build cache between runs. And it writes a Job Summary listing every Gradle command and its result.

Three details save you pain. The cache is written only from the default branch; other branches only read it. Do not also turn on `cache: gradle` in setup-java or add an `actions/cache` step for `~/.gradle`, because they get in the way of setup-gradle. And since CI runs `./gradlew`, it reads the same `gradle.properties`, so the build cache and configuration cache work there too.

Version 6 of setup-gradle changed the licensing. The default cache provider is closed-source: free for public repositories, a free preview for private ones, with paid tiers planned for large companies. To stay fully open source, set `cache-provider: basic`, an MIT-licensed provider built on `actions/cache`. hello-jvm's workflow has that line ready, commented out, for private repositories.

sections.h: A Dockerfile for a JVM app
sections.body:
The image needs a JRE and your jars, nothing more. The JDK, Gradle and the Kotlin compiler are build tools. That is the multi-stage pattern from Day 16, and hello-jvm's Dockerfile has two stages:

1. The build stage starts from `eclipse-temurin:21-jdk` and runs `./gradlew :app:installDist`. That task leaves `bin/app` (a start script) and `lib/` (every jar) in `app/build/install/app`.
2. The run stage starts from `eclipse-temurin:21-jre`, copies only that folder, adds a non-root user and a healthcheck, and starts `/app/bin/app`.

Layer order matters, as on Day 13. The wrapper files are copied and run first, so the layer that downloads Gradle (about 170 MB) stays cached until you change the Gradle version. The build line also uses a BuildKit cache mount: `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle/caches`. That folder of downloaded libraries survives between builds, even when the layer itself has to rerun after a code change. In our test, the first build downloaded everything; after a one-line change in `Main.kt`, the whole image rebuilt in 25 seconds with no downloads.

Two more things. The cache mount lives in your local builder, so a fresh CI runner starts with it empty; `cache-from: type=gha` still saves the Gradle layer. And on an Apple Silicon Mac, `docker build` makes an arm64 image. Both temurin images ship amd64 and arm64 variants, so add `--platform linux/amd64` when the image must run on amd64 servers.

sections.h: JVM memory in containers, and images without a Dockerfile
sections.body:
The JVM reads the container's memory limit and sizes its heap from it. By default the largest heap is only 25% of that limit. We checked in a 512 MB container: `MaxHeapSize` was 134217728 bytes (128 MB). With `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` it became 402653184 (384 MB). The Dockerfile sets that flag in `JAVA_OPTS`, which the start script passes to `java`. Stay well below 100%: threads, class metadata and the JIT need memory outside the heap. If the total crosses the limit, the kernel kills the container (Day 35 covers memory limits in Kubernetes).

You do not always need a Dockerfile. Three tools build the image from the build itself:

- Jib, a Gradle and Maven plugin from Google, for any JVM app.
- Spring Boot's `bootBuildImage` task, which uses Cloud Native Buildpacks.
- Quarkus container-image extensions, such as Jib, Docker and Podman.

Jib puts your dependencies and your classes in separate layers. The `jibDockerBuild` task loads the image into Docker, and the `jib` task pushes to a registry with no Docker at all. By default it uses an `eclipse-temurin` JRE base and builds for amd64 only.

Jib has a catch today. Version 3.5.4 does not work with the configuration cache, so you run it with `--no-configuration-cache`, and Gradle warns that the build will break on Gradle 10. For learning, the Dockerfile wins, because you can see every step. At work, use what your framework and platform team already use.

lessons.analogy: The build cache works like a coat check. When a task finishes, Gradle hangs its outputs on a hook and keeps the ticket: a fingerprint of everything that went in. When the same ticket comes up again, in any folder or on any machine that shares the cloakroom, Gradle hands back the coat instead of making a new one. Where it breaks: a coat check returns your own coat, while the build cache happily gives you outputs that another build made. That is safe only because the ticket covers every input.

code.title: Dockerfile
code.src:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- build stage: a full JDK runs the Gradle wrapper ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src

# 1. The wrapper on its own. This layer downloads Gradle itself, and Docker
#    reuses it until gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties changes.
COPY gradlew ./
COPY gradle/wrapper/ gradle/wrapper/
RUN ./gradlew --version --no-daemon

# 2. Everything the build reads: settings, flags, catalog, build logic, both projects.
COPY settings.gradle.kts gradle.properties ./
COPY gradle/libs.versions.toml gradle/
COPY build-logic/ build-logic/
COPY greeting/ greeting/
COPY app/ app/

# 3. Compile and package. The cache mount keeps downloaded dependencies between
#    builds, even when the source code changed. Tests already ran in CI.
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle/caches \
    ./gradlew --no-daemon --console=plain :app:installDist

# ---- run stage: only a JRE and the app ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
# installDist made bin/app (a start script) and lib/ (every jar the app needs).
COPY --from=build /src/app/build/install/app/ ./
# The version is baked in at build time: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0.0 .
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION
# The start script passes JAVA_OPTS to the JVM. Let the heap use up to 75%
# of the container's memory limit (the default is 25%).
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0"
# Run as a normal user, not root.
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1
# Exec form: the start script ends with exec, so the JVM becomes PID 1 and gets SIGTERM.
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/bin/app"]

code.src:
name: jvm-ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

# One run per branch or pull request. A new push cancels the older run,
# except on main, where every merge gets a full result.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

# The GITHUB_TOKEN in this workflow can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # A JDK to run Gradle. build-logic asks for a Java 21 toolchain,
      # so Gradle also uses this JDK to compile and test (no extra download).
      # Do not add "cache: gradle" here: setup-gradle does the caching.
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"

      # Checks gradle-wrapper.jar against known checksums, caches Gradle's
      # downloads (written on main, read on other branches) and adds a Job Summary.
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6
        # In a private repository, uncomment the next two lines to use the
        # open-source (MIT) cache provider instead of the default one.
        # with:
        #   cache-provider: basic

      # The same command you run on your laptop, with the same gradle.properties.
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./gradlew build

      - name: Upload test reports
        # Upload even when tests fail: that is when you need the report most.
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: test-reports
          path: "**/build/reports/tests/"
          retention-days: 7

  image:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - name: Build the image (no push)
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          tags: hello-jvm:ci
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ github.sha }}
          # Reuse image layers from earlier runs (GitHub Actions cache).
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

explain_back.prompt: Explain the difference between the build cache and the configuration cache in 3 to 4 sentences. Say what each one stores and what a hit looks like in the output.
explain_back.answer: The build cache stores task outputs, such as compiled classes and test results, under a key made from a hash of the task's inputs. When another build has the same inputs, even in another folder or on CI, Gradle copies the outputs back and marks the task FROM-CACHE. The configuration cache stores the task graph that the build scripts produced, so a repeat run can skip running the scripts. A hit prints `Reusing configuration cache.` at the start, and tasks then run or are skipped as usual.

interview.q: A Gradle build in CI is slow. How do you speed it up?
interview.a: First I look at which tasks actually ran, using the console output or a Build Scan. Then I make sure caching works: setup-gradle restoring Gradle User Home, the build cache turned on, and no `clean` in the CI command. Ideally there is also a remote cache that CI writes and laptops read. I turn on the configuration cache and parallel execution, and fix plugins that break them. If one project dominates, I look at compile avoidance: splitting modules and preferring `implementation` stops changes from rippling.

interview.q: How do you package a JVM service as a container image?
interview.a: With a multi-stage Dockerfile: a JDK stage runs the Gradle wrapper and `installDist`, and a JRE stage gets only the start script and jars. I copy the wrapper first so the Gradle download stays in a cached layer, and use a BuildKit cache mount for dependencies. The run stage uses a non-root user, an exec-form ENTRYPOINT so SIGTERM reaches the JVM, and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` so the heap fits the container limit. Jib or Spring Boot's `bootBuildImage` are good alternatives when a team prefers no Dockerfile.

interview.q: What is the difference between dependency locking and dependency verification?
interview.a: Locking records which versions were resolved, in a `gradle.lockfile`, so a build fails if the graph changes until someone updates the lock. Verification records checksums or signatures of the files themselves, in `verification-metadata.xml`, so a tampered or swapped jar fails the build. Locking guards against drift and surprise upgrades; verification guards against supply-chain tampering. You can use both together.

deeper.body:
The cache mount that made local rebuilds fast does not help much on a fresh CI runner. Each runner starts with an empty BuildKit cache, so the build stage downloads every library again whenever the source changed. In our test the mount held about 900 MB after one build: libraries, the Kotlin compiler, transformed jars and the local build cache. The `cache-from: type=gha` setting brings back image layers, including the 170 MB Gradle layer, but not the contents of a cache mount.

Teams handle this in one of three ways:

1. Accept it. For a small service, the image job takes a minute or two longer than it could. hello-jvm's workflow does this, because the Dockerfile stays simple and the same everywhere.
2. Build outside Docker, and only package inside it. The build job runs `./gradlew build :app:installDist` with setup-gradle's warm cache, and a one-stage Dockerfile copies `app/build/install/app` onto the JRE image. The trade-off is that the image now depends on what the runner built, so laptops and CI must use the same steps.
3. Use Jib in CI. It runs inside Gradle, so it shares setup-gradle's cache, and `jib` pushes without a Docker daemon. Today that means `--no-configuration-cache` for that step.

The configuration cache has a CI angle too. Gradle 9.1 added a read-only mode, `-Dorg.gradle.configuration-cache.read-only=true`, meant for builds that should use entries but not write them, such as pull request builds. And because entries can contain secrets, setup-gradle can encrypt them in the GitHub Actions cache with a key you give it. Make one with `openssl rand -base64 16`, store it as a repository secret, and pass it as `cache-encryption-key: ${{ secrets.GRADLE_ENCRYPTION_KEY }}`.

Finally, the remote build cache is where large teams win the most time. The setup-gradle documentation recommends the usual pattern: CI builds push to the remote cache and switch off the local one, and local builds then read what CI wrote. The same pattern works with Develocity or any other HTTP build cache server.

recap: The Gradle Wrapper pins one Gradle version per project, so always run `./gradlew`.
Every run has three phases; build scripts set up tasks, and only task actions do the work.
Gradle skips a task whose inputs and outputs did not change (UP-TO-DATE) or copies its outputs from the build cache (FROM-CACHE).
Default to `implementation`; use `api` only for types that appear in your public functions.
A version conflict resolves to the highest version, and `dependencyInsight` tells you why.
A version catalog names versions in one file; a BOM moves a family of libraries together.
Convention plugins in a `build-logic` included build replace copied build logic.
In GitHub Actions, setup-java plus setup-gradle give you wrapper validation and caching; `cache-provider: basic` keeps it fully open source.
Ship JVM apps on a JRE image with the `installDist` output, a non-root user and `MaxRAMPercentage`.

flashcards.front: Which four files make up the Gradle Wrapper?
flashcards.back: gradlew, gradlew.bat, gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar and gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties. Commit all four.

flashcards.front: Name Gradle's three build phases in order.
flashcards.back: Initialization (settings), configuration (build scripts and task graph), execution (task actions).

flashcards.front: Which part of a registered task runs at execution time?
flashcards.back: Only the doLast (or doFirst) actions. The rest of the register block runs during configuration.

flashcards.front: What does UP-TO-DATE mean on a task line?
flashcards.back: Gradle compared the task's inputs and outputs with the last run, found no change, and skipped it.

flashcards.front: What does FROM-CACHE mean on a task line?
flashcards.back: The task's inputs matched a build cache entry, so Gradle copied the outputs in instead of running it.

flashcards.front: Which two tasks does `build` run?
flashcards.back: assemble (makes the outputs) and check (runs the tests and other checks).

flashcards.front: implementation or api: which reaches the compile classpath of consumers?
flashcards.back: api. implementation stays private at compile time and only reaches consumers at runtime.

flashcards.front: How does Gradle resolve a version conflict by default?
flashcards.back: It picks the highest requested version for the whole graph.

flashcards.front: Which command explains why a library has a certain version?
flashcards.back: ./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --dependency <name> --configuration runtimeClasspath

flashcards.front: Where does the version catalog live, and how do scripts use it?
flashcards.back: gradle/libs.versions.toml; build scripts refer to entries as libs.<name> and libs.plugins.<name>.

flashcards.front: What does platform(...) add to a build?
flashcards.back: A BOM: recommended versions for a family of libraries, so they move together.

flashcards.front: Where should setup shared by many projects live?
flashcards.back: In a convention plugin inside a build-logic included build, applied by id.

flashcards.front: Configuration cache or build cache: which stores the task graph?
flashcards.back: The configuration cache. The build cache stores task outputs.

flashcards.front: How do you see which JDKs Gradle can compile with?
flashcards.back: ./gradlew -q javaToolchains. The build's jvmToolchain(21) picks one, not the java in your terminal.

flashcards.front: In GitHub Actions, which action should own Gradle caching?
flashcards.back: gradle/actions/setup-gradle. Do not also use setup-java's cache: gradle or actions/cache on ~/.gradle.

flashcards.front: How do you keep setup-gradle v6 caching fully open source?
flashcards.back: Set cache-provider: basic, the MIT-licensed provider built on actions/cache.

flashcards.front: What is the JVM's default maximum heap inside a container?
flashcards.back: 25% of the container's memory limit. Raise it with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.

flashcards.front: Which task produces bin/ and lib/ for a container image?
flashcards.back: installDist from the application plugin, in app/build/install/app.

flashcards.front: Why does Jib 3.5.4 need --no-configuration-cache?
flashcards.back: Its task reads project at execution time, which the configuration cache does not allow.

flashcards.front: Dependency locking or verification: which checks file checksums?
flashcards.back: Verification (gradle/verification-metadata.xml). Locking pins which versions resolve (gradle.lockfile).

quiz.q: Which command should a CI job use to build a Gradle project?
options: `gradle build`
`./gradlew build`
`mvn package`
`./gradlew build --rerun-tasks`
quiz.why: The wrapper runs the Gradle version the project pins, so CI matches every laptop; rerunning all tasks only wastes time.

quiz.q: A task is `tasks.register("count") { val n = fileTree("src").files.size; doLast { println(n) } }`. When does Gradle count the files?
options: Only when the doLast action runs
Every time any Gradle task runs
When the task is configured, before execution
Only the first time the wrapper runs
quiz.why: Everything in the register block outside doLast runs while Gradle configures the task, which happens before execution.

quiz.q: You fix a typo inside a function body in library `core`. `app` depends on `core`. Which task is most likely UP-TO-DATE on the next build?
options: `:app:compileKotlin`
`:core:compileKotlin`
`:core:jar`
`:app:test`
quiz.why: core's public API did not change, so compile avoidance skips recompiling app, while core itself and app's tests still run.

quiz.q: `./gradlew :app:dependencies` shows `guava:31.0-jre -> 33.2.1-jre`, but app's build file says 31.0-jre. Why?
options: Gradle always fetches the newest release
The catalog silently overrides build files
31.0-jre was removed from Maven Central
Another dependency needs 33.2.1-jre, and highest wins
quiz.why: Two paths requested different versions, and Gradle's default conflict resolution picks the highest.

quiz.q: You want to upgrade Kotlin for every project in hello-jvm with one edit. Which file do you change?
options: `gradle.properties`
`gradle/libs.versions.toml`
`gradle-wrapper.properties`
`app/build.gradle.kts`
quiz.why: The catalog's kotlin version feeds the Kotlin Gradle plugin that the convention plugin applies to every project.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile does `COPY . .` and then `RUN ./gradlew installDist`. Every code change downloads Gradle again. What is the best fix?
options: Add `--no-daemon` to the RUN line
Switch the build stage to a JRE image
Copy and run the wrapper in an earlier layer
Delete the .dockerignore file
quiz.why: A layer that only depends on the wrapper files stays cached across code changes, so Gradle is downloaded once.

quiz.q: Your pull request builds never save anything to setup-gradle's cache. Why?
options: By default only the default branch writes the cache
Pull requests cannot use the Actions cache at all
Caching only works with `cache-provider: basic`
Gradle turns caching off when a test fails
quiz.why: setup-gradle writes the cache from the default branch and only reads it elsewhere, which fits GitHub's cache scoping rules.

quiz.q: You set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100` in a container with a 2 GB limit. What is the risk?
options: The JVM refuses to start with that value
The heap can never grow past 512 MB
Docker ignores JVM flags in containers
Total memory passes 2 GB and it gets killed
quiz.why: Threads, class metadata and the JIT use memory outside the heap, so a heap as large as the limit pushes the process over it.

quiz.q: hello-jvm's Dockerfile ends with `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/bin/app"]`, and the start script ends with `exec java ...`. Why does `docker stop` finish in under a second?
options: The JRE image ships a faster kernel
Java becomes PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
Docker sends SIGKILL to Java at once
The healthcheck stops the app first
quiz.why: Exec form plus exec in the script leaves java as process 1, so it gets the SIGTERM, runs its shutdown hook and exits with code 143.

quiz.q: In jvm-ci.yml the `image` job has `needs: build`. What does that do?
options: image starts only after build succeeds
Both jobs start at the same time
image runs on the same runner as build
build is skipped when image fails
quiz.why: needs makes a job wait for the listed jobs and skips it if they fail, so no image is built from code that failed its tests.
